analysis.one_liner: Rewrote federal labor law to ease union organizing, mandate first contracts, and give public employees bargaining rights.
analysis.headline: Bernie Sanders' sweeping pro-union labor law rewrite drew zero cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the nation's main labor law to make union organizing much easier: unions could be certified on signed cards instead of secret-ballot elections, a union could impose a first contract through binding arbitration, and employers would face steep new penalties, reinstatement of fired workers during legal proceedings, treble damages, and possible loss of federal contracts for willful labor-law violations. It would also end the federal protection for state right-to-work laws, create national collective bargaining rights for all state and local government employees, let workers at U.S. companies' foreign operations file complaints against the U.S. parent, and give workers equal representation on the boards of their pension plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Private-sector workers who want union representation would get certification by signed cards, an enforceable first contract, and real penalties for employers who fire or intimidate union supporters. Public employees in the roughly half of states without broad collective bargaining rights would gain them nationwide, including a limited right to strike. Union organizations would gain members and dues. Workers of U.S. multinational companies abroad, and participants in single-employer pension plans, would also gain new rights.

how_it_helps.text: Would let the National Labor Relations Board certify a union once a majority of workers signed recognition cards, replacing the often-delayed secret-ballot election process with a faster route to representation.

Would give a union the option of sending a first contract dispute to compulsory binding arbitration if no agreement is reached within 45 days of certification, ending the strategy of stalling negotiations indefinitely.

Would create real financial consequences for labor-law violations: minimum $10,000 civil penalties per willful violation, mandatory injunctions, reinstatement of fired workers pending the case, make-whole compensation, treble damages for workers injured by unlawful discrimination, and debarment of willful violators from federal contracts for up to three years.
Would repeal the provision of the Taft-Hartley Act that lets states ban union-security agreements, ending federal protection for state right-to-work laws.
Would repeal prohibitions on secondary strikes, boycotts, and hot cargo agreements, restoring unions' ability to pressure companies across an entire supply chain rather than only the direct employer.

Would create a National Public Employment Relations Commission giving all state and local government employees nationwide the right to organize and bargain collectively, with a right to strike limited only by public health and safety (firefighters and public safety officers barred from striking).

Would let workers at U.S. companies and their subsidiaries in free-trade-agreement countries file unfair labor practice complaints against the U.S. parent company, extending American labor standards beyond U.S. borders.

Would require single-employer pension plans to be governed by joint boards of trustees with equal worker and employer representation, and let participants elect worker trustees when no union designates them.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the main costs: union organizing without a secret-ballot election, contracts imposed by arbitrators, exposure to secondary boycotts, minimum $10,000 penalties per willful violation, treble damages, and possible federal contract debarment. State and local governments, and ultimately taxpayers, would face federally mandated bargaining and binding arbitration with all public employees, potentially raising public payrolls. U.S. multinationals would face labor claims from operations abroad, and single-employer pension plan sponsors would share control of plan assets with worker trustees.

drawbacks.text: Certifying unions on signed cards alone would eliminate the secret-ballot election, a safeguard both employers and some union skeptics consider important for a free choice; critics of card check argue it invites pressure on workers to sign in front of organizers or peers.

Binding arbitration of a first contract would let a third-party arbitrator set wages and work rules after only 45 days of bargaining, taking final terms out of both sides' hands and removing employer leverage in initial negotiations.

Repealing the ban on secondary boycotts and hot cargo agreements would allow union pressure campaigns to target neutral businesses that merely do business with the employer in dispute, potentially raising costs and disrupting firms uninvolved in the labor conflict.

The bill would override state choices in two ways: ending federal protection for state right-to-work laws, and imposing federal collective bargaining and arbitration rules on all state and local governments, preempting existing state public-sector labor laws.

Requiring joint trusteeship of single-employer pension plans would give unions or elected participants equal control over plan assets that employers currently control, adding governance obligations and shared fiduciary liability for plan sponsors.

The bill had zero cosponsors in either party across the entire two-year Congress, signaling that even labor-friendly Democrats did not attach their names to this broad a rewrite, and giving it no visible path to consideration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains for workers — faster union certification, enforceable first contracts, and meaningful penalties for labor-law violations — are large and address a real problem: union election and first-contract delays are widely used to outlast organizing drives. But the tradeoffs are serious and honest supporters would acknowledge them: abolishing secret-ballot elections removes a worker protection, imposed first contracts hand wage-setting to arbitrators, and legalized secondary boycotts pull uninvolved businesses into disputes. The bill also took a maximalist approach — folding in right-to-work repeal, a national public-sector bargaining regime, foreign operations, and pension trusteeship — at a time when it could not attract a single cosponsor, so breadth cost it any chance of narrow, passable reforms.

outcome.mechanism: Sanders introduced the bill, the House sent it to its labor committee, the committee sent it to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernie Sanders, then the House's only independent, introduced the Workplace Democracy Act on June 23, 1997.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day; the committee never considered it further.
On July 31, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the Congress.
Not a single other member of the House cosponsored the bill at any point in the two-year Congress.
The bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, leaving federal labor law unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, particularly nonunion companies and right-to-work states, are better off because the bill died: none of the mandates it would have imposed — card-check certification, arbitrator-written first contracts, legalized secondary boycotts, or national public-sector bargaining — ever took effect. The Republican-led committee that declined to act also preserved the labor-law status quo without ever having to vote on it.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor for its entire two-year life; no other member joined him.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. William Goodling (R-PA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 23, 1997 and never held a hearing or markup on it, passing it down to a subcommittee.

against.name: Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations
against.role: Subcommittee of referral, chaired by Rep. Harris Fawell (R-IL)
against.what_they_did: Took the referral on July 31, 1997 and took no action for the remaining year and a half of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Controlled the House floor calendar in the 105th Congress under Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-GA)
against.what_they_did: Never brought any labor-law expansion to the House floor; the leadership sets what reaches a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only one independent sponsor and a Republican-led committee that never acted, leaving the partisan split unmeasurable.

industries.note: The bill would remove the secret-ballot election as the gate to union representation, allow arbitrators to impose first contracts, and add minimum $10,000 penalties per willful violation, treble damages, and federal contract debarment. Its core effect is to shift bargaining power from employers to workers, and employers would bear the direct cost.

Card-check certification, repeal of right-to-work protections, legalized secondary boycotts, and a national public-sector bargaining regime would all grow union membership, bargaining scope, and dues revenue. The unions' institutional gain runs alongside the gains for the workers they would represent.

Title II would force every state and locality to bargain with all public employees under a new federal commission, with binding arbitration available and preemption of state labor laws. Public employees would gain rights, but taxpayers could face higher payroll costs from arbitrator-imposed contracts.

Their foreign subsidiaries in free-trade-agreement countries would become subject to National Labor Relations Act claims against the U.S. parent, extending American labor standards to overseas operations.
The bill would require joint trusteeship of single-employer pension plans, forcing employers to share control of plan assets equally with union-designated or elected worker trustees.
